Round 2: With Achilles leaving, Athena (and any other gods / goddesses giving Achilles their personal attention, barring Thetis who, being Achilles' mother and also technically a nereid instead of a goddess, wouldn't care about the war now that her son's gone) transfers her protection to another Grecian hero; who receives her protection, and how do the tides of battle turn?

Ultimately, it was Odysseus that came up with the winning strategy for the Greek forces. Even without Achilles, the Greeks would still win. Odysseus was a badass.

While Odysseus was undeniably clever, I am not entirely certain that he was technically required, or that he would be able to procure a victory without Achilles. Furthermore, I think that you're downplaying the roles that other heroes played; for instance, Ajax the Great is also a contender for someone who could have ended the war without Odysseus if we're really going to play the game of "who steamrolls over the opposition".

Firstly, let's talk about why Achilles is technically required for a Grecian victory; remember, after Achilles left the field, Hector had led a sally that rushed all the way to the Grecian ships; the only reason that they were held back was because of Ajax, who leaped from ship to ship slaughtering Trojans like a god of war and preventing them from setting fire to the ships; but even with Ajax's efforts, he couldn't fight an army and Hector at the same time, and it was stated that it was only a matter of time until he was overwhelmed. This was the Grecian force's most desperate hour, and it was ultimately solved when Achilles lent the Grecian forces his aid in the form of Patroclus, who donned Achilles' armor and bluffed the Trojan forces into retreating. If Achilles had left, Patroclus would have followed; at the very least, the Trojans would have known, and the "fake Achilles" ploy would not have worked, causing a Grecian defeat as Hector cuts off the tip of Ajax's spear, burning the ships and effectively the Grecian supply line.

Furthermore, the removal of Hector was crucial to Odysseus' success. Hector was described as Agamemnon the leader and Achilles the warrior rolled into one; with his intelligence and tactical skill, it is questionable whether the Trojan Horse would have succeeded under his watchful eye.

Finally, I think there's an assumption that Odysseus was the only one who had the abilities to end the war; I don't think that's a fair assumption. Ajax once fought Hector into a stalemate, showing that he was at least the equal of Hector in battle if not in leadership; with both Achilles and Hector gone, Ajax could have easily dominated the field as no one else came close to his level of godliness in combat. Odysseus' cunning plan was only required as his selfishness had led to Ajax's suicide, forcing the war back into a stalemate.

Overall, in order for the Grecian forces to win, Hector had to be disposed of before he got to the Grecian ships; and given that the only other Grecian hero able to fight Hector was Ajax, and even Ajax was ultimately pressed into losing when he was overwhelmed by pure numbers, the outcome of the war might look less certain than you think.

Edit: After some further thought, I think that there might be a possibility that even Hector would be fooled by the Trojan Horse (though I do think it would be unlike him to be that careless, it's not outside of the realms of possibility), However, I still maintain that an alternative method would be needed to protect the Grecian supply lines, and the Achilles appeared to be the only one capable of doing that.

In my opinion, Round 2 would go solidly to the Greeks on one provision - the one to receive divine protection must be Ajax the Great.

Ajax the Great is most notable for being one of the very few heroes who never sustained a wound throughout the entire Trojan War. He is all the more notable for having completed this feat despite never earning the support of a God. He is described as being of immense stature and unyielding courage, and is most memorable for his gigantic seven-layered shield of ox-hide and bronze, and he is also arguably the most powerful line of defense on the Grecian side.

Ajax also fought Hector thrice, and the score was essentially even despite the gods clearly favouring Hector on every occasion. On the first time, Ajax had stunned and wounded Hector in a duel, but Hector, under the watchful eye of Zeus, is given sufficient strength to fight on till the heralds of Zeus called an end to the battle, pronouncing a draw - in spite of the fact that Ajax was uninjured while Hector was injured. Clearly, the gods favoured Hector in pronouncing this draw, and more so in giving Hector strength while not aiding Ajax in any way.

On the second occasion, Ajax the Great was single-handedly holding off the entire Trojan army with his enormous spear; Hector attempts to disarm Ajax in order to allow his men to burn the Grecian ships, but is instead gravely wounded by a giant rock that Ajax throws onto him; Hector is carried away from the field on the brink of death, and is only saved from dying by Apollo.

On the third occasion, Hector once again returns to the field after Apollo revives him; this time, Zeus watches over the battle and allows Hector to disarm Ajax, even though Ajax could not be injured; but nevertheless, deprived of his spear, Ajax is no longer able to hold back the Trojan army, and retreats from the field uninjured.

As a reminder, Ajax completed all of this despite holding no favours from any of the Gods. It is in fact arguable that, even if Hector received divine aid, given enough time, Ajax would be able to defeat Hector on a one-on-one duel. Notice that Ajax's only defeat was when he was mobbed by Trojan forces, and that furthermore even then he was able to retreat completely uninjured. With the favour of a God by his side, I believe that Ajax would be able to comfortably defeat anyone in the war, and would be much harder to kill than Achilles as well.
